It was in the inner pocket, dead, because the room's security field killed live audio within three metres of the north wall; he had filed that complaint himself, twice, and lost both times.
His thumb found the power button as the screen came up grey and slow.
Ruth saw it.
Her face did not go angry.
That was the worst of it.
Her face went *tired*, the way it went when a junior engineer brought her a result she'd been dreading.
"Strike that," she said, clearly, evenly, at a volume that carried.
"I misspoke.
The seeding program was for particulate dispersal — industrial haze mitigation.
That's the record.
That's always been the record."

citedContext.text: "Then you understand the constraints."
"I understand there's a mechanism.
I want to know who signed it in 1968 and I want to know who's signing the renewals now."
He put the memo on her desk, face up, her name at the top.
"You're on the renewal chain.
That's your initials in green."
Ruth did not look at it.
She had her reading glasses off and her hands folded, and she looked the way she had looked on the north wall: tired, unangry, a woman bringing forward a result she had already priced.
"Before you say the next sentence," she said, "hear mine.
As of this morning the atmospheric program is being placed under external review.
I've recommended a full audit of the seeding contracts.
I've also recommended that the filter team be led by someone who understands the network from the inside — someone with the standing to see the audit through."
She let a beat pass.
"That's a directorship, Soren.
North Wall.
The review answers to you."
"And the memo?"
"Becomes part of the audited record, which is sealed for the duration of the review."
"Which is how long?"
"However long it takes to do it properly."
She said it without flinching.
"You want to burn it down.
I understand that.

But the masks are the only thing keeping this city upright today, and the masks are *mine*, and the filter team is *yours*, and if you hand that memo to a newsroom this afternoon then by midnight the only institutions left standing in Kestrel will be the ones that don't need electricity."
